prize_parts.citation: for the invention of the magic-wavelength optical lattice clock and its realization at the 10^-18 level of fractional uncertainty

statement.case_for: I am moving my preferred configuration from B008 to B035, alone. In round 1 I said I would not defend B008 against a well-argued shift to the clocks, and the exchange has supplied that argument. My own concern was novelty: the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 ion-control prize cover much of the enabling toolkit. Lindroth, Mehlig and Danielsson answered this on physical grounds. The magic-wavelength condition lets a large ensemble of neutral atoms be held in the Lamb-Dicke regime without shifting the clock transition, so statistical power comes from many atoms interrogated in parallel, which a single-ion clock cannot do. That is a different step, not a refinement, and it is the kind of idea one can state in a single sentence of a citation. The result is also verified in the way I value most as a computational physicist: several independent laboratories (JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, PTB, SYRTE, NIST) reproduce uncertainties near 10^-18 and compare clocks against each other, which is a stricter test than most theoretical constructs ever face. Consequences are already concrete in tests of constancy of fundamental constants, dark-matter searches and relativistic geodesy. Finally, all eight members proposed the same two names, so the credit structure of idea (Katori) plus frontier realization (Ye) is not in dispute, which is not true of any other part on the shortlist.
statement.case_against: My reservations are real and I record them. Lattice clocks are a precision-measurement achievement rather than a new phenomenon, and a sceptic can still read them as the next increment after 2005 and 2012. Lemonde, Takamoto, Lisdat and the Sr and Yb groups at SYRTE, PTB and NIST contributed materially and sit outside two names. The redefinition of the second is under discussion but not decided, so the strongest societal consequence is still pending. On pure conceptual reach I continue to think B008 is the bigger idea: a topological classification of band structures changed how materials are searched for and understood, and I do not retract that. What changed my preference is not that the clock is the larger science but that B008 cannot be given a defensible three-name credit: Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed the HgTe route that Molenkamp measured, Zhang is deceased, the three-dimensional generalisation lies outside the names, and the 2016 prize leaves a fair argument about overlap. A prize should not rest on a credit list that the historical record does not support. I would not combine B035 with B008, because Kane, Mele and Molenkamp would exceed the three-person limit.

responses.point: Lindroth ranked clocks first but called B008 the most serious competitor on conceptual breadth, said she would not oppose it if the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang question could be resolved, and argued that the comb prize honoured a tool the clock uses, not the clock itself.
responses.response: I agree with the distinction between the comb as a counting tool and the lattice clock as a new interrogation scheme, and that is the point that moved me on the novelty worry. I also agree that B008 is the larger idea, so we are not far apart on the science. Where I come down differently from your hedge is on the credit: I do not think the committee can resolve the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang question within three names this year, because it is a matter of history and not of wording. I therefore conclude that B035 is the prize we can defend, and I leave B008 as the principal alternative for a future cycle in which the credit question might be settled.

responses.point: Mehlig moved from B008 to B035, still regards topological band theory as more far-reaching than the clocks, and argued against squeezing B008 into three names the historical record does not support.
responses.response: We agree on both the ranking of ideas and the credit problem, and I now follow you to the same conclusion. Your suggestion to draft the citation around the specific invention, many neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength so the lattice does not perturb the transition, with 10^-18 as the demonstrated consequence, is the right defence against the objection that it reads as a sequel to 2005 and 2012, and I have written my citation that way. I would also record, as you propose for the Sr and Yb groups, that the topological work is left unrewarded this year for credit reasons and not for lack of merit.

responses.point: Kroll argued that a clock is an instrument whose conceptual novelty is easy to underrate, that the magic-wavelength condition is a real idea, and that neutral-atom lattice clocks are not covered by the 2005 or 2012 prizes.
responses.response: You are right about my own bias. I rated clocks low in the opening partly because I tend to rank concepts above instruments, and your point that independent verification between laboratories at 10^-18 is a stricter test than many theoretical constructs have passed is fair, including for the theory side where I work. I also accept that neither earlier prize covers neutral-atom lattice interrogation. I still hold that the citation must name the lattice clock specifically, so that the wording answers Ye's credit question you and Mehlig raised and does not drift into a general metrology prize.

responses.point: Olsson kept B008 as her first alternative but argued that the 2016 prize already recognised the underlying topological framework, that the HgTe proposal is the bridge the three credited names cannot express, and that the clock has no live dispute about what was measured.
responses.response: I take the 2016 point more seriously than I did in round 1. I still think the Z2 time-reversal-invariant case is distinct from the Haldane-type and phase-transition work honoured then, but I agree it makes the novelty argument sharper for B008 than for the clocks, and that when credit and overlap are both open the risk compounds. You said you would move B008 up if colleagues showed the credit could be framed around the Z2 invariant and its first observation. I tried to make that argument in round 1 and, having heard Mehlig, Danielsson and Johansson, I no longer think it succeeds, so I am not asking you to move it.

responses.point: Johansson answered my opening ranking of the clocks, said the performance gain of orders of magnitude is measured and the idea original, and described the circuit QED discount from the 2025 prize.
responses.response: Your disagreement with my low opening rank was justified, and I have moved. On B004 I stay where I was in round 1: as Chair last year I am wary of a second circuit prize so soon, and Girvin and Huang are missing from the theory credit. I note your own disclosure and your own concession that the discount may fade over a few years. That is a reason to keep B004 as an alternative for a later cycle, not to rank it above the clocks now.

responses.point: Pearce proposed a second part for IceCube, crediting Halzen alone, while flagging the one-name credit as a compromise and his own proximity through Fermi-LAT.
responses.response: I respect the observational-window argument and the 2002 precedent, and I appreciate that you flag the one-name credit and your proximity yourself. I do not support the second part. Crediting Halzen alone leaves Karle and Spiering out on a judgement the supplied text does not settle, source identification is still at modest significance, and the chair's own summary shows nobody else endorses the part. A shaky one-name part would weaken a prize whose strength is its clean attribution. I would prefer B035 to stand alone and B023 to return in a later year.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept lattice clocks as a distinct invention from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, and whether the citation wording on the magic-wavelength lattice and many-atom interrogation is enough to say so.
Whether a two-name prize is fair to the Sr and Yb groups at SYRTE, PTB and NIST, and to the ion-clock groups, which I cannot verify from the supplied text.
How close the redefinition of the second must be for the societal consequence to count as settled; I treat it as supporting and not necessary.
Whether my abandonment of B008 is premature: if the committee could agree a credit that handles Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, I would reconsider it for a future cycle.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. My electronic-structure and magnetism work is adjacent to B008 and B051, which I disclosed as a possible bias toward them, and moving away from B008 is against that bias. I have no documented personal or institutional connection to Katori or Ye, or to any credited name on the shortlist. I served as Chair for the 2025 cycle, which concerned superconducting circuits, and I have said that this makes me cautious about B004; this is a judgement on timing, not a conflict.
